overview: This file brings together a 1932 cross-reference and a 1934 consular despatch transmitting English translations of two Japanese colonial regulations governing aliens in Taiwan. Although filed under immigration and head tax, the surviving documents concern admission, passports and visas, temporary residence, police registration, lodging reports, exclusion, deportation, penalties, and exemptions rather than a head tax. The translated measures are Taiwan Government General Order No. 7 of February 1918 and General Order No. 71 of July 1899, illustrating how Taiwan’s rules differed from those prevailing in Japan proper.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Ketcham despatch from Taihoku
subfiles.about: A filing note directs readers to another decimal-file location for Ketcham’s despatch concerning Taiwan’s immigration laws and regulations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to despatch No. 1-1127 from Ketcham at Taihoku, dated November 15, 1932. It states that the despatch transmitted information concerning Taiwan’s immigration laws and regulations and directs the reader to file 800.504/36.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 43 transmitting Taiwan alien-entry and residence regulations
subfiles.about: Garrels transmits translations of Taiwan’s regulations governing the admission and residence of aliens in response to a State Department request for special immigration reports.
subfiles.summary: Garrels reports that the American Vice Consul in Taihoku has supplied copies and translations of Taiwan’s alien-entry and residence regulations, which differ from those in Japan proper. He encloses the translations in response to the Department’s instruction of September 14, 1934. According to the Vice Consul, the regulations apply equally to temporary visitors and aliens entering for gainful employment, with no special restrictions for the latter category.

subfiles.title: Translation of Taiwan Government General Order No. 7 on entry of aliens
subfiles.from: Taiwan Government; translated by C. Matsuo
subfiles.about: The regulation establishes documentary requirements and grounds for refusing or reversing an alien’s landing in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The order permits the governor or a prefectural chief to deny landing to aliens lacking valid travel documents or considered dangerous to imperial interests, public order, morals, public health, or the public purse. Passports or nationality certificates ordinarily required a photograph and a Japanese diplomatic or consular visa issued within the preceding year, subject to reciprocity-based exemptions. Aliens had to produce their documents and answer police inquiries truthfully; fraud or misuse could result in exclusion and deportation. Diplomats, consular personnel, foreign officials, their families, and crews of foreign vessels were exempted.

subfiles.title: Translation of Taiwan Government General Order No. 71 concerning treatment of aliens
subfiles.from: Taiwan Government; translated by C. Matsuo
subfiles.about: The regulation creates a police-administered system for reporting, registering, monitoring, and deporting aliens residing or lodging in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The order requires householders and lodging proprietors to report foreign guests to the police, while longer-term foreign residents must register themselves, their families, addresses, occupations, and other personal details. Police stations were to maintain registers of foreigners, which members of the public could inspect or copy upon payment of specified fees, and foreigners could be required to answer questions and produce passports or nationality documents. The Governor General could deport persons lacking means of support, itinerants, beggars, threats to public order or morals, and deportees who reentered without permission; noncompliance and false reports carried imprisonment or fines. Chinese were excluded from several provisions and were instead governed by separate regulations where such rules existed.

interest: The file is useful for studying the distinctive immigration and police regime imposed in colonial Taiwan and its differences from the system in metropolitan Japan. The two translated orders reveal how entry control was linked to public health, poverty, political security, morality, household surveillance, and compulsory registration, while also showing exemptions for diplomats, consular personnel, ship crews, and—under separate legal arrangements—Chinese residents. The translations by a U.S. consular interpreter also document how American officials gathered and circulated foreign immigration law during the interwar period; notably, the surviving contents contain no substantive head-tax provision despite the file title.
